Clark's nutcracker, a gray-and-black relative of crows and jays, lives in the high mountains of western North America. In late summer it pulls seeds from pine cones, carrying as many as about a hundred at a time in a pouch beneath its tongue. It buries most of them in the ground, a few seeds in each hiding place. Field studies suggest that a single bird may store well over 20,000 seeds in a season, spread across thousands of separate caches, and then live on them through the winter and into spring, often digging through snow to reach them.

Recovering so many caches might seem to require luck rather than memory, since a bird could simply probe the ground wherever pines grow. Experiments in the early 1980s argued against that view. Nutcrackers that buried seeds in a large indoor room later found their own caches far more often than chance would predict. When a researcher moved the stones and logs on the floor, the birds tended to dig at spots shifted by about the same distance, which suggests they located caches by their positions relative to landmarks.

The birds' forgetting also matters to the forest. Seeds that are never recovered may sprout, and the whitebark pine, whose cones do not open on their own, depends largely on the nutcracker to spread its seeds. Researchers have also reported that food-storing birds tend to have a larger hippocampus, a brain region involved in spatial memory, than related species that do not store food.

On the evening of August 21, 1986, a large cloud of gas burst from Lake Nyos, a deep crater lake in the volcanic highlands of northwestern Cameroon. The gas was mostly carbon dioxide, which is heavier than air, so instead of rising it flowed down the surrounding valleys, displacing the air near the ground. People and animals in its path suffocated, some of them many kilometers from the lake. About 1,700 people died, along with thousands of cattle. Two years earlier, a smaller release at Lake Monoun, roughly 100 kilometers away, had killed 37 people.

Most investigators concluded that the disaster was not a sudden eruption of lava. Instead, carbon dioxide from magma deep below had been seeping through springs into the bottom of the lake for a long time. Because Lake Nyos is deep and its layers rarely mix, the gas built up in the cold bottom water, held in solution by the weight of the water above, much as gas stays dissolved in a sealed bottle of soda. Something then disturbed the layers, and as gas-rich water rose, the falling pressure released the gas in a rush. Whether that trigger was a landslide, heavy rain, or something else is still debated.

Since 2001, engineers have installed pipes that reach down to the lake bottom. Once water begins rising through a pipe, the gas coming out of solution keeps it flowing upward, so the system needs no pumps to keep running and releases the gas slowly and harmlessly.

In the late sixteenth century, astronomers, navigators, and surveyors spent long hours multiplying and dividing long numbers by hand, and every step invited error. In 1614 the Scottish landowner John Napier published a book describing a new aid, which he called logarithms, after roughly twenty years of work. Its central idea was that numbers could be paired with other numbers in such a way that multiplying two of the originals corresponded to adding their partners. With a table of these pairs, a long multiplication became two lookups, an addition, and a final lookup.

Napier's tables were awkward to use, however, partly because of the system on which he had built them. The English mathematician Henry Briggs traveled to Scotland to meet him, and the two agreed that tables based on powers of ten would be more convenient. Briggs spent years computing them, and in 1624 he published logarithms of the numbers from 1 to 20,000 and from 90,000 to 100,000, to fourteen decimal places. The Swiss clockmaker Jost Bürgi had developed a similar method independently, but his tables appeared only in 1620 and attracted far less notice.

The new method spread quickly. Johannes Kepler used logarithms in preparing his tables of planetary motion, published in 1627, and in the 1620s the English clergyman William Oughtred is usually credited with designing the slide rule, which performed the same trick with sliding scales. Much later the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace reportedly remarked that logarithms had doubled the lives of astronomers by shortening their labors.

Most flowers release their pollen easily: a visiting insect brushes against the anthers, the pollen-bearing parts, and grains stick to its body. Thousands of plant species, however, keep their pollen sealed inside anthers that open only through a tiny pore at the tip. Tomatoes, potatoes, eggplants, and blueberries are among them. Measuring the distance to a star is a hard problem. A faint star might be a dim one nearby or a brilliant one very far away, and its appearance alone does not say which. In the early twentieth century a way around this problem emerged from routine work at the Harvard College Observatory, where Henrietta Swan Leavitt was employed to examine photographic plates and record the brightness of stars.

Leavitt studied plates of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a star cloud visible from the Southern Hemisphere, taken at Harvard's station in Peru. She identified hundreds of variable stars, which brighten and dim in a regular cycle. Among one type, now called Cepheids, she noticed that the brighter stars took longer to complete each cycle. Because all the stars in the Cloud are at roughly the same distance from Earth, differences in how bright they appeared had to reflect real differences in the light they gave off. In 1912 she published the relationship for twenty-five such stars: the longer the period, the more luminous the star.

The relationship turned Cepheids into markers of distance. An astronomer who measured a Cepheid's period could estimate its true brightness and, by comparing that with how bright it looked, work out its distance. First, though, the scale had to be fixed using Cepheids close enough to measure by other means, and early estimates were later revised. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble found Cepheids in the Andromeda nebula, showing that it lay far beyond the Milky Way.

In April 1721 a ship arriving from the Caribbean brought smallpox to Boston. The minister Cotton Mather had read reports, published in London by the Royal Society, describing a practice called inoculation used in Constantinople: material from a smallpox sore was placed in a small cut in a healthy person's skin, usually producing a mild case that left the person immune. Mather had also heard of it from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man in his household, who said he had been inoculated as a child and that the practice was common where he came from.

Mather urged Boston's physicians to try the method, and only one, Zabdiel Boylston, agreed. In June he inoculated his own six-year-old son and two enslaved members of his household. Many townspeople were alarmed, since an inoculated person could pass the disease to others, and William Douglass, the town's only physician with a university medical degree, attacked the practice as reckless. In November someone threw a lit bomb through Mather's window; it failed to explode.

Boylston went on to inoculate about 240 people and kept careful records. Of these, six died, roughly 2 percent. Among the nearly 6,000 Bostonians who caught smallpox in the ordinary way, about 14 percent died. Boylston's figures, later published in London, are often cited as an early use of numerical comparison to judge a medical treatment, although the inoculated had not been chosen at random and may have differed from other patients in health.

Klein, a discount store.

In the 1850s Chicago was one of the fastest-growing cities in the United States, but it stood on flat, marshy ground only a few feet above the level of Lake Michigan. Water had nowhere to drain. Streets turned to deep mud after rain, cellars flooded, and waste collected in standing pools. Outbreaks of cholera, including a severe one in 1854, strengthened calls for a sewer system.

The engineer Ellis Chesbrough, hired in 1855, faced an obvious difficulty: sewers need a slope so that waste can flow by gravity, and the ground was too low for pipes to be buried deep enough. His plan reversed the usual order. Sewer pipes were laid on the surface along the middle of the streets and then covered with earth, so that the streets themselves were raised, in places by several feet or more. Buildings were left below the new street level, and their owners had to fill in their lots or lift the buildings up. Michelangelo's David, completed in Florence in 1504, was carved from a block of marble that other sculptors had already tried and abandoned. The block, quarried at Carrara, had been assigned in the 1460s to Agostino di Duccio for a figure meant to stand high on one of the buttresses of the city's cathedral. He began roughing it out but stopped, and a later sculptor, Antonio Rossellino, gave up the commission soon after receiving it. For roughly twenty-five years the tall, narrow block lay exposed to the weather in the cathedral workshop's yard.

In 1501 the cathedral's overseers offered it to Michelangelo, then about twenty-six. Working within a block that was already partly cut, he turned its narrowness to advantage: David stands with his weight on one leg and his body slightly turned, a pose that suits the slab's shallow depth. Some art historians think the large head and hands reflect the original plan to view the statue from far below, where such features would look in proportion.

In January 1504 a committee of artists and officials, reportedly including Leonardo da Vinci and Sandro Botticelli, met to choose a site, and the statue was set up beside the entrance to the Palazzo della Signoria, the seat of the city's government. It remained there until 1873, when it was moved indoors to protect it, and a copy now stands in its place.
